title: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Sri Aurobindo

cards.b:
In the 19th century, Indians faced a hard question: how should we respond to British power and Western ideas?

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan said Muslims must embrace modern education and cooperate with the British to rise again.

Sri Aurobindo said India must reject foreign rule outright and draw strength from its own spiritual tradition.

The syllabus pairs them, so expect questions on each and on how they differ.

Sir Syed came from a Mughal noble family in Delhi and worked as a judicial officer for the East India Company. During the revolt of 1857 he stayed loyal to the British and saved British lives at Bijnor.

After 1857, the British blamed Muslims for the revolt. Muslims were falling behind in education and government jobs.

Sir Syed set out to rebuild trust with the British and to modernise Muslim society. His essay Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (The Causes of the Indian Revolt, 1859) blamed British policy, especially the lack of Indians in the legislature.

• He founded the Scientific Society (1864) to translate Western works into Urdu.
  • He started the journal Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870) to spread social reform.
  • He founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875. It became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

He argued that Islam and science do not conflict. The Quran, the word of God, cannot contradict nature, the work of God. This rational approach was called naturalism; his opponents mocked him as a "nechari".

Early on, Sir Syed called Hindus and Muslims "two eyes of the beautiful bride that is India".

Later, he opposed the Indian National Congress (founded 1885). In speeches at Lucknow and Meerut in 1887–88, he argued that in elections the Hindu majority would dominate, and that Muslims should keep away from Congress agitation.

Many historians see this as an early form of the two-nation idea. Others say he spoke of separate communities with distinct interests, not separate nation-states. Pakistan's founders later claimed him as a forerunner.

Aurobindo Ghose was educated in England, at St Paul's School and King's College, Cambridge. He returned to India in 1893 and served the Maharaja of Baroda.

He became a leader of the Extremists in Congress, during the protests against the Partition of Bengal (1905). He wrote for the paper Bande Mataram.

He was tried in the Alipore Bomb Case (1908–09) and acquitted. After a spiritual experience in jail, he left politics in 1910 and moved to Pondicherry. The Sri Aurobindo Ashram there was formally founded in 1926, with the Mother.

cards.h: New Lamps for Old and boycott
cards.b:
In his articles "New Lamps for Old" (1893–94), Aurobindo attacked the Moderates' petitions and loyalty to Britain as politics of begging.

His essays on passive resistance (1907) set out a plan: boycott of British goods, schools, courts and administration, and building national alternatives in their place.

He also said that if the British met passive resistance with violence, the people had a right to defend themselves.

His goal was complete independence, purna swaraj, long before Congress adopted it in 1929.

For Aurobindo, the nation was not just land and people. It was a living mother, a form of divine power, or shakti.

Nationalism is a religion that has come from God.
Paraphrase of his Bombay speech, 1908

Later, in The Ideal of Human Unity and The Human Cycle, he looked beyond the nation toward a spiritual unity of humanity, through free nations working together.

• Aim: Sir Syed wanted Muslim uplift within British rule. Aurobindo wanted complete freedom from it.
  • Method: Sir Syed chose education and loyalty. Aurobindo chose boycott and mass resistance.
  • Source: Sir Syed used Western reason. Aurobindo used Indian spirituality.
  • Critique: Sir Syed's later views fed communal separation. Aurobindo's Hindu imagery could exclude Muslims, though he himself opposed communal politics.

Sir Syed's work grew into the Aligarh movement, a broad effort to modernise Muslim society.

  • The Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) spread modern schools across India.
  • He wrote a commentary on the Quran using reason, and urged Muslims to read it afresh rather than rely only on traditional scholars.
  • He supported the English language as the key to jobs and knowledge.
  • He criticised polygamy, but defended purdah and moved slowly on women's education.

Aligarh trained a new Muslim middle class. Many of its graduates later led the Muslim League (1906). Others, like the Ali brothers, joined the Khilafat and national movements.

His critics among the ulema of Deoband (founded 1866) rejected his Western leanings.

Aligarh Muslim University remains a major institution. In 2024, a seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court overruled the 1967 Azeez Basha judgment, which had denied AMU minority status. The Court left the final decision on AMU's status to a regular bench.

Aurobindo's birthday, 15 August, is also India's Independence Day. He gave a message to the nation that day in 1947.

Auroville near Pondicherry, founded in 1968, carries his vision of human unity.

"Discuss Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's views on education and politics."
"Examine Sri Aurobindo's idea of spiritual nationalism."
"Was Sir Syed a communalist or a modernist?"

Structure: context of 1857 and Bengal partition, then each thinker's life, method and key ideas. Give a balanced reading of Sir Syed's "two nations" remarks. Compare them in a short table or list.
